snip.t: Renal peritubular fibroblasts (EPO‑producing cells): Synthesize erythropoietin in response to hypoxia via HIF‑2α signalling.
Special groups: sickle cell disease (hydroxycarbamide, folate, vaccines, prompt treatment of crises), pregnancy (iron and folate supplements), chronic kidney disease (erythropoietin).
Pallor: Suggests anemia, common in chronic kidney disease (CKD) due to reduced erythropoietin.

qs.q: A patient with renal cell carcinoma presents with erythropoietin-driven polycythaemia. Which of the following is another well-known paraneoplastic manifestation of this tumor?
o: Hyponatremia due to primary cortisol loss
qs.e: Renal cell carcinoma can secrete parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP), leading to hypercalcaemia alongside polycythaemia and hypertension. Hypocalcaemia and primary adrenal loss are not standard paraneoplastic features of this malignancy.

qs.q: A child presents with a normocytic anemia and significantly reduced erythropoietin production secondary to chronic renal failure. What is the expected reticulocyte response?
qs.e: Anemia resulting from reduced erythropoietin production in renal failure is associated with an inadequate bone marrow response, manifesting as a low or normal reticulocyte count. Elevated reticulocytes would indicate hemolysis or acute bleeding.

qs.q: A healthy term neonate transitions to extrauterine life, establishing normal spontaneous respiration. What is the primary trigger that prompts the rapid downregulation of erythropoietin production immediately following birth?
o: Sudden drop in circulating fetal hemoglobin levels
Depletion of maternal iron stores in the liver
Increased blood oxygen content and tissue delivery
Rapid destruction of fetal red blood cells
qs.e: The onset of respiration increases oxygen saturation and blood oxygen content, which directly causes the downregulation of erythropoietin production. This process is triggered by oxygen delivery rather than red cell destruction or iron depletion.

qs.q: A 52-year-old woman has fatigue, pruritus after hot showers, headaches, and facial plethora. Hgb is 18.5 g/dL, Hct 58%, WBC 14,000, platelets 520,000. Serum erythropoietin is very low. JAK2 V617F mutation is detected. Most likely diagnosis?
o: Renal cell carcinoma with EPO secretion
qs.e: Elevated RBC mass + elevated WBC and platelets (panmyelosis) + very low EPO + JAK2 V617F mutation + aquagenic pruritus = polycythemia vera. Low EPO distinguishes it from secondary polycythemia where EPO is elevated.

o: Peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney
qs.e: Peritubular interstitial cells in the renal cortex sense hypoxia via HIF-1α and release EPO to stimulate red cell production.

ai.title: Erythropoietin in Clinical Practice
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Erythropoietin is a kidney‑derived hormone that stimulates red cell production. In low‑resource settings its deficiency underlies anaemia of chronic disease and CKD. Clinicians must recognise causes, test appropriately, and manage with iron and recombinant EPO while monitoring for complications.

sections.p: Erythropoietin (EPO) is produced by renal peritubular fibroblasts in response to tissue hypoxia via HIF‑2α signalling. Low serum EPO indicates impaired renal production or resistance.
b: Serum EPO <10 IU/L in anaemia suggests renal failure or chronic disease

t.b: Assess iron stores; <100 ng/mL indicates iron deficiency, >500 ng/mL suggests inflammation
Estimate GFR; CKD stages 3–5 are associated with low EPO
Defines anaemia severity; <10 g/dL in CKD warrants EPO therapy

sections.p: Anaemia severity is graded by haemoglobin: mild 10–11.9 g/dL, moderate 8–9.9 g/dL, severe <8 g/dL. CKD staging uses eGFR: stage 3 (30–59), 4 (15–29), 5 (<15).
b: Stage 3 CKD often has mild anaemia; stage 5 usually severe anaemia

sections.p: In East Africa, the top causes of low EPO are chronic kidney disease (often from hypertension, diabetes, or glomerulonephritis), HIV‑associated nephropathy, and schistosomiasis‑related renal damage.
Patients have pallor, fatigue, dyspnoea, and sometimes tachycardia. In CKD, symptoms may be subtle; anaemia can worsen chronic disease symptoms.
b: Pallor of conjunctiva and mucous membranes

sections.p: Baseline workup includes CBC, reticulocyte count, serum ferritin, transferrin saturation, serum creatinine, and urine albumin. When unavailable, a simple urine dipstick for protein and a basic CBC can guide initial management.

t.b: Low in EPO deficiency; high in haemorrhage or hemolysis

sections.p: Rapid drop in haemoglobin, uncontrolled hypertension, or new onset of pulmonary oedema in a patient on EPO therapy warrants urgent review.
b: EPO over‑replacement can cause hypertension and thromboembolism

sections.p: Treat underlying kidney disease, correct iron deficiency with oral or IV iron, and start recombinant EPO if haemoglobin <10 g/dL and iron stores adequate. Monitor haemoglobin every 2–4 weeks.
b: Avoid high‑dose EPO to prevent hypertension

t.b: Ensures erythroid precursors receive iron; improves EPO response
Stimulates erythropoiesis; dose adjusted to haemoglobin target

sections.p: Regular monitoring of haemoglobin, iron status, and renal function is essential. Preventive measures include blood pressure control, infection prophylaxis, and vaccination.
b: Vaccinate against hepatitis B and pneumococcus

sections.p: Anaemia of chronic disease can mimic iron deficiency anaemia; both present with low ferritin but differ in transferrin saturation and inflammatory markers.
b: Inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR) are elevated in ACD

sections.p: Serum ferritin is an acute‑phase reactant; it may be normal or high in inflammation despite iron deficiency. Urine dipstick protein may miss microalbuminuria.
b: Use transferrin saturation to confirm iron deficiency

whenToSeekHelp: Severe drop in haemoglobin (<5 g/dL), sudden onset of chest pain or dyspnoea, uncontrolled hypertension (>180/110 mmHg) while on EPO

faq.q: Why is iron required with EPO therapy?
faq.a: EPO stimulates red cell production; iron is the substrate for haemoglobin synthesis, so deficiency limits response.

faq.q: Can EPO be used in malaria‑related anaemia?
faq.a: No, malaria causes haemolysis and iron sequestration; EPO is ineffective and may worsen inflammation.

faq.q: What is the target haemoglobin in CKD patients on EPO?
faq.a: Aim for 10–11.5 g/dL to balance anaemia correction with risk of hypertension and thrombosis.

exam: A 45‑year‑old HIV patient with CKD stage 4 presents with fatigue. What is the first investigation you order? — CBC, reticulocyte count, serum ferritin, and creatinine to assess anaemia type and iron status.
A patient on recombinant EPO develops sudden hypertension. What is the most likely complication and how do you manage it? — EPO‑induced hypertension; reduce dose and add antihypertensive.
A 60‑year‑old woman with CKD stage 3 has haemoglobin 9.2 g/dL and ferritin 80 ng/mL. What is the next step? — Start oral iron; reassess haemoglobin in 4 weeks.
A child with sickle cell disease has anaemia. Why is EPO therapy generally avoided? — Sickle cell anaemia is due to haemolysis; EPO does not address the underlying crisis and may increase viscosity.
A patient with chronic kidney disease has low EPO but normal ferritin. What does this suggest? — EPO deficiency due to renal failure, not iron deficiency.
A patient on EPO therapy develops a sudden drop in haemoglobin. What should you suspect? — Possible haemorrhage or haemolysis; check reticulocyte count and bleeding sources.
A patient with CKD is on EPO and develops a thrombotic event. What is the likely mechanism? — Excess erythrocytosis increases blood viscosity, predisposing to thrombosis.
